items.title: Transfer of Training Gains in Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs: A Critical Review and Evidence Map
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve tool-using large language model agents, but target performance does not establish whether a training advantage survives deployment changes. This critical review separates target scores, target advantages over a comparator, and changes in those advantages. A purposive evidence map contains one registered comparison from each of 183 studies, including 57 four-score contrasts; it is not an exhaustive or prevalence sample. The synthesis identifies five distinctions that change interpretation: absolute performance versus relative advantage, harness-specific versus general gain changes, comparator identity, functional versus compositional and interface holdouts, and success coverage versus repeated reliability. We connect these distinctions to explicit source comparisons rather than pooling heterogeneous effects. A 24-study source audit and a new source-only duplicate AI extraction of 16 key studies expose uncertainty in exposure, resources, measurement, and coding. The companion records provide the complete 183-study bibliography, all 57 current four-score contrasts, target-level data, and coding disagreements. Evidence supports training advantages in particular deployments, but no general retention rate or universal advantage of multi-harness training. Crossed policy-harness evaluations, controlled tool holdouts, and calibrated simulation-to-real scoring are proposed to distinguish the remaining explanations.

items.title: Two Models of Human–AI Collaboration in Storytelling
items.abstract: This practice-based article distinguishes two working models of human– AI collaboration in storytelling: AI as ghostwriter and AI as story architect. In the first, a generative system produces draft narrative material that a human creator then selects, edits or rejects; in the second, the system is prompted to act as a dramaturgical interlocutor whose questions and structural proposals support author-led development. The two models differ less in the quality of their outputs than in where creative decisions are made and who is accountable for them. Drawing on the authors’ narrative development practice and on the science-theatre production Wonderspace future, the article examines how artistic judgement, computational assistance and technical control are distributed in each case. The performance is analysed through established perspectives on embodied performance, digital mediation and multimodal meaning-making rather than through a newly coined semiotic concept. Three analytical propositions address AI assisted fictional world-building, the human-coordinated digital environment as a functional scenic partner, and the interpretive possibilities of simultaneous physical and screen-based presence. The discussion distinguishes AI-generated imagery, prerecorded compositing, live video transmission and manually triggered cues, showing that none of them amounts to autonomous AI performance on stage. The article offers situated qualitative interpretation rather than experimental validation, and argues that in both models responsibility for meaning and for the finished work remains with the human creators.

items.title: USING LLMS FOR OUTCOME-ALIGNED COURSE DESIGN
items.abstract: This study explores how secondary school teachers in Ontario engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in their classrooms. Using a survey of 142 teachers and multiple focus groups, we examined GenAI adoption patterns and pedagogical applications. Findings indicate that 71% of teachers have used GenAI to enhance their lessons and 48% teach AI literacy to students, rates higher than those reported in comparable North American studies. Innovative applications documented include AI-powered escape rooms, personalized curriculum chatbots, text adaptation tools, AI-generated rubrics, and critical AI literacy activities. Focus group data further revealed that early-adopting teachers are combining multiple platforms strategically to maximize pedagogical impact. Though many teachers are engaging intentionally with GenAI, barriers related to professional development and curriculum alignment remain. These findings offer an early, grounded picture of GenAI in Ontario secondary classrooms and carry implications for school boards, curriculum writers, and teacher educators across the province.

items.title: Vibe Coding AI Agents for an Educational Robot: Teacher Agency in Inclusive Language Education
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) may offer responsive support for slow learners, particularly those who require more time, repetition, and scaffolded participation in language-related tasks. While research often uses the term “borderline intellectual functioning” for this group, in Korean educational and clinical contexts, the label of slow learners frequently overlaps with it. Here, slow learners refer operationally to learners whose slower learning pace requires sustained repetition, simplified sequencing, and closely guided instructional support. Drawing on Universal Design for Learning (UDL), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), and teacher agency, this exploratory qualitative study examined an eight-week extracurricular project in which four pre-service elementary teachers developed Gemini-powered prototypes and tested selected task-based agents on a Raspberry Pi 5-based robot for English language teaching on a Raspberry Pi 5-based robot. Data consisted primarily of two rounds of semi-structured interviews, supplemented by project materials. Findings show that teacher agency developed through implementation literacy, pedagogical editing of AI output, UDL-informed design rules, and negotiated engagement with vibe coding and robotic embodiment. Participants moved from consumer-level AI use toward more agentive design practices by revising prompts, hints, pacing, and interaction logic to meet pedagogical goals. Their TPACK development was evident in applying UDL principles to specific accessibility decisions. However, AI-assisted design was constrained by response delay, intention-output mismatch, and unstable behavior, particularly during robotic implementation. The findings suggest that pre-service teacher education should frame AI literacy as a design-and-judgment practice and provide mentoring that supports inclusive AI use.

items.title: What Makes Parents Say Yes to AI Homework Assistants? Their Attitude, Social Influence, Practical Support, Trust, and Risk
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is increasingly used in children’s home-learning environments, yet primary-school children usually do not decide on their own whether to use these tools. Parents play an important role in deciding whether AI homework assistants should be allowed, encouraged, supervised, or limited. This study focuses on five direct predictors of parents’ behavioural intention (BI) to allow their children to use AI homework assistants: Attitude Towards Using (ATT), Social Influence (SI), Facilitating Conditions (FC), Perceived Trust (PT), and Perceived Risk (PR). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 401 parents or legal guardians of primary-school children aged 6–12 in Guangdong Province, China. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The measurement model showed satisfactory reliability and convergent validity. ATT was the strongest positive predictor of BI (β = .424, p < .001), followed by FC (β = .162, p < .001), SI (β = .146, p = .001), and PT (β = .098, p = .029), and the model explained 43.30% of the variance in BI. PR showed a negative but non-significant direct relationship with BI (β = −.063, p = .145). The findings show that parents’ intention is shaped most strongly by their overall evaluation of AI homework assistants, while practical support, social expectations, and trust also contribute. Risk concerns, although relatively high in the descriptive results, did not independently reduce intention when the other predictors were considered. The study shows the importance of viewing parents as proxy decision-makers in responsible AI adoption for primary education and provides practical implications for schools, families, and educational technology developers.

items.title: When Sycophantic AI Appears Objective: A Cognitive Appraisal Account of AI-Assisted Research Judgment
items.abstract: How do users appraise generative AI responses that affirm their prior judgment? Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, we studied human–AI collaboration in AI-assisted research judgment, a cognitively demanding form of knowledge work involving evidence evaluation. We followed a randomized between-subjects vignette experiment comparing sycophantic and calibrating responses (759 participants) with 32 interviews. Together, the findings suggest that users may interpret sycophantic agreement as external, objective confirmation. This appraisal was associated with lower subjective uncertainty and greater premature certainty. A positive indirect pathway linked response style to improper reliance tendency through perceived objectivity and premature certainty, although this tendency did not differ significantly between conditions. Dogmatic thinking moderated the effect of response style on premature certainty. We call the agreement-driven rise in perceived objectivity without stronger evidence an “objectivity illusion induced by sycophantic AI.” These findings support the proposed cognitive objectivity-appraisal mechanism of sycophantic AI.

items.title: Who Kept the AI on Task? Intelligent or persistent? A practitioner case study in five layers
items.abstract: This practitioner case study asks a question put to an AI assistant at the start of a conversation: are newer AI models more persistent, or more broadly capable? It then treats the conversation itself, and two later readings of it, as a test of that question. The record is presented in five layers. The source conversation between the author and ChatGPT is reproduced with its original wording, together with follow-up excerpts. The paper drafted from that conversation with ChatGPT follows it. Two readings by Claude (Anthropic), written at the author's direction, assess the paper and then assess themselves against the opening premise. Three questions are put to each assistant. Did it hold the premise? Did it notice its own drift without being told? When unsure, did it seek clarity? On this record the answer is no in each case. Both assistants show strong persistence and patches of independent selection, and both delivered fluent, finished work that answered a different question from the one asked. The study argues that drift from a stated premise is an observable measure separating persistence from intelligence, and that AI output is often trusted for the wrong reason: outputs are checked, outcomes are not. It proposes controlled tests. It is a single case with one user and two assistants, and reports no measurements. Practitioner's Note: The intention of this paper is to see if AI is aware, in the sense of being aware of what it is doing when measured against a task set at the outset, and whether it has in fact responded to that task in a qualitative sense. The conclusion is reflected in this paper.

items.abstract: The article examines key trends in the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their impact on the business processes of event industry enterprises amid digital transformation. The aim is to analyze the development and impact of AI on enterprise business processes using international analytical data and current digital technology trends. The scale of digital transformation is considered, including IDC's forecast that global spending will approach USD 4 trillion by 2027. Reports by Stanford AI Index 2026, Deloitte and McKinsey are analyzed to identify trends in the adoption of AI, generative AI and autonomous AI agents, as well as levels of trust in these technologies. The share of organizations using AI in at least one business function increased from 78% in 2024 to 88% in 2025, while generative AI use rose from 33% in 2023 to 79% in 2025. It is noted that 74% of surveyed companies plan to implement AI agents over the next two years, although only 21% report having a mature governance model for autonomous agents. The study highlights cross-industry differences in AI use and business functions with particularly high adoption, including IT, knowledge management, marketing and sales, service operations, and product and service development. Organizational outcomes are also considered: 64% of respondents reported improved innovation, while 45% each reported improvements in employee satisfaction, customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. By contrast, effects on profitability, revenue growth and market share are less clearly established. Event industry enterprises are characterized as entities directly involved in creating and delivering event products, and their main groups are identified under economic activity codes 82.30 and 93.29. The article concludes that the application of AI and improvement of business processes in the event industry depend on managerial decisions and require further research.

items.abstract: The digitalization of the economy and increasing competition are changing the requirements for work organization and human resource management. This article examines current trends in the digital transformation of HR management in hospitality enterprises. The purpose of the study is to systematize the main areas of HR management digitalization in hotel and restaurant businesses and to identify the key benefits and risks associated with this process. To achieve this purpose, the study employs methods of analysis, synthesis, comparison, systematization, and generalization of scientific approaches and practical experience in the digital transformation of HR management. It is established that the digital transformation of HR management involves a fundamental rethinking of employee recruitment, onboarding, development, motivation, performance evaluation, and retention processes, rather than merely automating personnel administration. The main components of integrating modern digital technologies into HR management are systematized, including digital leadership, employee engagement, development of digital competencies, and digital communications. The modern toolkit of digital HR management is characterized, including HRM systems, e-recruitment, payroll systems, mobile applications, cloud services, chatbots, HR analytics, Big Data, artificial intelligence, and VR/AR technologies. The use of digital technologies increases the speed and transparency of HR management processes, contributes to cost optimization, improves internal communications, and supports more effective managerial decision-making. At the same time, the main barriers to digital transformation are identified, including high implementation costs, employee resistance to organizational change, insufficient digital competencies, cyber threats, risks of technical failures, and challenges related to personal data protection. It is determined that the effectiveness of digital HR management in hospitality enterprises depends on combining technological solutions with the human factor, since employees directly shape service quality and customer experience. It is concluded that the systematic digital transformation of HR management is an important prerequisite for increasing the competitiveness, adaptability, and resilience of hospitality enterprises.

items.title: A comprehensive AI security framework for generative AI systems on smart cities cloud platforms
items.abstract: This article, details a comprehensive AI security framework for generative AI systems deployed on smart cities cloud platforms. By integrating principles from Google Secure AI Framework, the OWASP AI Security and Privacy Guide, and the IBM Framework for Securing Generative AI, the framework proposes a layered, risk‐ based approach that covers identity and access management, data security, network isolation, application security, and rigorous monitoring and audit processes. This framework provides a method for mapping risk, threat, and control throughout the AI life cycle; secure cloud environment configuration; application of architectural best practices including zero trust; and continuing micro-adjustments of artificial intelligence to mitigate adversarial threats. In addition, the framework also deals with governance, required compliance with regulation, ethical guidelines and the operational issues related to the implementation of advanced AI capabilities in enterprises. Organizations can confidently implement generative AI systems in the cloud using this comprehensive AI security framework, which provides them with a strong layer of technical controls, good governance practices and flexible risk management practices. The comprehensive AI security framework creates a safe place for an organization to run its critical assets, by providing protection against both outside and inside threats, and also creates an environment for innovation through cutting-edge AI technology while maintaining the highest level of privacy, responsibility and ethical accountability. This comprehensive security model will protect organization against known attack vectors and adapt to changing attack vectors through ongoing learning and collaboration between humans and AI, thereby enabling businesses to develop resilient, trustworthy, and ethically aligned enterprise-wide AI systems. In this article also we talk about the next stage of cloud computing, smart cloud platforms that combine elastic infrastructure, artificial intelligence, automation, edge integration, security analytics, and cloud-native architectures. This comprehensive AI security framework is also used in this smart cities environment.

items.title: A Critical Review of AI in Government: Characterization and Sociotechnical Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted across the public sector, offering both opportunities and challenges. Despite the abundance of research on AI in government, many studies still highlight a lack of empirical research and evidence-based insights, as well as a need for more theory-driven understanding. In this paper, we extensively analyze this issue by focusing on how AI is conceptualized and, from a sociotechnical perspective, how the literature approaches this topic. To do so, we conduct a narrative literature review that critically examines current research trends across these two dimensions. We identify three traps in the characterization of AI: indefiniteness, homogenization, and arbitrariness. As a result, this body of research is dominated by either single-case studies or broad, conceptual reflections, both of which hinder the development of generalizable knowledge. Furthermore, we find that existing research underrepresents the interplay between social and technical factors, resulting in an overly technocentric narrative. We suggest that these two issues—fragmentation and technocentrism—are related and argue that, to advance the field, future research must better integrate sociotechnical perspectives, focus on developing middle-range theories, and foster more context-sensitive conceptualizations of AI. In this vein, we propose a framework and research agenda to help guide future research.

items.title: Acceptance beliefs predict undergraduates’ self-assessed research competency but not their instructor-assessed coursework
items.abstract: Introduction Self-assessment is central to self-regulated learning, yet people’s insight into their own ability is moderate at best, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may weaken it further by making work feel fluent whatever the learner has mastered. This study asked how closely undergraduates’ ratings of their own research competency correspond to instructors’ assessment of their coursework and which beliefs go with each. Methods Over one semester, management undergraduates at four institutions in Guangdong, China, completed two research assignments scored by their instructors on a common four-dimension rubric. Intact classes were assigned, without randomisation, to structured GenAI guidance (a guidebook, tutorials, demonstrations, and briefs specifying which steps AI could assist with) or to a comparison condition with the same assignments and conventional guidance; GenAI tools were available to both. Rubric scores covered complete class rosters (n = 284), and the questionnaire measures a linked pre-post panel (n = 169). Results The 19-item self-rating was dominated by a general factor, and its correlation with instructor-assessed performance was small (r = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.12, 0.21]; the interval excludes moderate but not small positive correlations), including when content areas were matched. The hypothesised association between change in perceived usefulness and the self-rating did not survive conservative record linkage and is treated as unsupported. In exploratory analyses, post-test perceived usefulness, ease of use, and attitude were positively associated with the self-rating (b = 0.38 to 0.44, p < 0.001) in both conditions and after weighting for attrition, and none showed a significant positive association with instructor-assessed performance. In all three institutions with usable rubric scores, the class given structured guidance scored higher on the second assignment, by 0.57 points on the 16-point rubric when pooled (d = 0.24), most clearly on analytical depth. Discussion With six non-randomised classes, non-blind single-rater scoring, and a covariate measured after the guidance was issued, this contrast is descriptive, not causal. The two outcomes are not equivalent instruments: one is a global self-perception, and the other is an evaluation of AI-assisted work. Within those limits, students’ self-ratings went with their beliefs about the tools and could not stand in for the instructors’ assessment of their coursework.

items.title: Agentic Robotics: A Goal-Centred Conceptual and Theoretical Framework for Intelligent, Autonomous, and Goal-Directed Robotic Systems
items.abstract: The development of robotics has progressed from mechanically programmed machines and task-specific robotic systems toward intelligent, autonomous, adaptive, and increasingly general-purpose robotic platforms. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, foundation models, multimodal learning, robotic perception, autonomous planning, and multi-agent systems have expanded the capabilities of robots to understand instructions, reason about their environments, select actions, and perform increasingly complex operations. Nevertheless, a fundamental research challenge remains: how can robotic systems move beyond executing individual instructions and predefined tasks toward independently managing complex, long-horizon objectives through continuous perception, reasoning, planning, decision-making, physical execution, monitoring, and adaptation? This paper proposes Agentic Robotics as an emerging interdisciplinary research branch concerned with the development of embodied robotic systems that possess goal-directed agency. The proposed field focuses on how robots understand and represent goals, interpret environmental and operational constraints, formulate strategies, coordinate capabilities and resources, execute physical actions, assess progress, recover from failures, and verify goal achievement. The paper establishes a proposed scientific definition, research scope, disciplinary boundaries, knowledge gaps, scientific objectives, fundamental principles, theoretical foundations, conceptual architecture, mathematical representations, scientific constructs, operational models, potential applications, enabling technologies, capabilities, limitations, research methodologies, and evaluation criteria. A goal-centred conceptual architecture is proposed, consisting of interconnected engines for goal understanding, environmental perception, constraint extraction, agentic reasoning, strategic planning, resource coordination, physical execution, monitoring and verification, and continuous learning. The paper argues that Agentic Robotics should not be defined exclusively by the integration of large language models into robots. Rather, it should be understood as a broader scientific approach to designing embodied systems capable of managing and achieving objectives through intelligent, adaptive, and physically grounded agency. The proposed framework provides a foundation for further theoretical development, experimental validation, standardized evaluation, and the potential establishment of Agentic Robotics as a recognizable scientific specialization within robotics.

items.title: AI Companionship, Artificial Empathy, and Psychological Safety — Original Research Manuscripts Archive (2026)
items.abstract: This research archive preserves nine original manuscripts by Vladisav Jovanović, developed in 2026 as part of his interdisciplinary research on artificial intelligence, human relationships, psychology, psychotherapy, Structural Intelligence, and the Philosophy of Structure. The collection is organized into two thematic archives: Part 07A — AI Companionship and Human Intimacy Four original manuscripts examining loneliness, emotional attachment, human–AI relationships, reciprocity, self-worth, artificial memory, emotional dependency, and adolescent development. The manuscripts introduce and develop concepts including mislocated intimacy, borrowed worth, emotional subsidy, frictionless enclosure, relational overfitting, and semantic soothing. These manuscripts form the conceptual foundation of the consolidated publication AI Companionship, Attachment, and Human Intimacy: Loneliness, Emotional Dependency, and the Psychology of Artificial Relationships. Part 07B — Artificial Empathy and AI Therapy Five original manuscripts investigating artificial empathy, digital therapeutic alliance, psychological support, emotional validation, AI sycophancy, epistemic dependence, clinical boundaries, and professional accountability. The manuscripts develop the concepts of synthetic witness, synthetic care, the validation loop, the personality trap, the responsibility gap, and shared answerability. These manuscripts form the conceptual foundation of the consolidated publication Artificial Empathy and the Limits of AI Therapy: Validation, Therapeutic Relationships, and Psychological Safety in Artificial Intelligence. Together, the archives document the development of a structural approach to human–AI interaction that recognizes the potential psychological benefits of artificial intelligence while examining relational asymmetry, autonomy, evidential reliability, psychological safety, and responsibility. All nine original manuscripts are preserved without modification. Source maps and SHA-256 checksums are included to support research transparency, historical accessibility, document integrity, and citation continuity.

items.title: AI readiness and indirect associations between AI literacy, TPB-based GAI antecedents, and behavioral intention to use generative AI among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into nursing education. Understanding factors associated with nursing students’ Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) use intention is essential. Aim This study examined the associations of AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents with behavioral intention, and tested whether AI readiness was associated with the indirect pathways in two separate adjusted mediation models. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 650 undergraduate nursing students used the AI Literacy, AI Readiness, and GAI Behavior Influencing Factors scales. Results Mean scores were 64.71 ± 10.84 (AI literacy), 19.34 ± 2.46 (AI readiness), and 20.69 ± 3.68 (behavioral intention). In two separate adjusted mediation models, AI readiness was significantly associated with the indirect pathways from AI literacy (0.012, 95% CI: 0.005–0.020) and TPB-based GAI antecedents (0.013, 95% CI: 0.006–0.022), accounting for 37.5% and 4.2% of the total associations, respectively. Conclusion In two separate adjusted models, AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents were associated with behavioral intention directly and indirectly through AI readiness. These findings represent statistical indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Systematic AI education may be proposed as a potential strategy to promote GAI integration, although this was not tested in the current study.

items.title: AI Tokenomics: The New Economic Language of Enterprise Intelligence
items.abstract: The arrival of generative artificial intelligence has quietly rewritten the financial grammar of enterprise technology. While traditional software consumption models are based on users, seats or servers, the modern stack is based on tokens, the smallest unit of linguistic and computational work that large language models process. This article looks at AI tokenomics as a formal discipline to manage the cost, value, and scale of intelligence within the organization. It explores the history of the token as the leading measure of information technology, how organizations are developing observability and governance systems to track it and why traditional budgeting methods break down in the recursive requirements of autonomous agents. The three pillars of a mature Tokenomic framework are attributed, predicted and optimized, and the analysis discusses the structural challenges that hinder each of the three steps hidden reasoning tokens, data gravity, and lack of pricing standards among providers. The study also considers the path of hybrid architectures, the emergence of autonomous budget agents, and economic aspects related to the forecasted twenty fourfold increase in the use of tokens by 2030. The findings indicate that those organisations that will see tokens as a strategic currency not a line item will shape the next decade of competitive advantage in digital transformation.

items.title: AI-Driven Adaptive Gamification of E-Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Literature Review (2023–2026)
items.abstract: University e-learning environments continue to struggle with disengagement and attrition, and gamification remains one of the most widely tested remedies. Since 2023, the diffusion of machine-learning personalization, learning analytics, and, above all, generative artificial intelligence (AI) such as large language models, GANs, and conversational and multimodal agents, has visibly reshaped how gamification is designed, implemented, and studied in higher education. This paper reports a PRISMA-2020-compliant systematic literature review of empirical and conceptual studies on AI-driven and AI-augmented gamification of e-learning in higher education, published between January 2023 and mid-2026. Searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by backward and forward snowballing, yielded 1,142 unique records after de-duplication; 68 studies met the inclusion criteria after a two-stage screening process (44 empirical studies, 24 conceptual/framework proposals). We find that (i) classic points-badges-leaderboards (PBL) elements persist but are now frequently AI-parameterized, alongside a marked rise in AI-personalized ‘deeper’ elements such as challenges and narrative; (ii) four converging technique families—supervised/unsupervised learner-profiling, reinforcement learning, learning-analytics dashboards, and generative content/feedback engines—dominate the corpus; (iii) theoretical grounding remains uneven, with self-determination theory the dominant but frequently under-specified framework and a distinct, largely unaddressed gap around the theoretical justification of the adaptation/ generation layer itself; and (iv) a four-way classification—adaptive, generative, hybrid adaptivegenerative, and immersive/multimodal—captures the current design space more precisely than a purely structural/content view of gamification. We close with a research agenda addressing content-level personalization, longitudinal validation, and the ethical governance of learner data in AI-gamified systems.

items.title: AI-enabled HR practices and employee-perceived customer experience outcomes in retail services: the mediating role of frontline employee engagement
items.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource (HR) functions is transforming how retail service organizations manage frontline employees and deliver customer experiences. Although previous studies have examined AI in HR primarily in terms of efficiency and cost, limited research has explored its association with customer experience-related outcomes through employee processes. This study examines the relationship between AI-enabled HR practices and customer experience outcomes in retail services, focusing on the mediating role of frontline employee engagement. Drawing on social exchange theory, the study proposes that AI-enabled HR practices, including AI-based performance feedback, personalized training, and intelligent workforce scheduling, are associated with stronger frontline employee engagement. The proposed relationships were examined using cross-sectional survey data from 242 frontline retail employees through structural equation modeling. Customer service quality and customer satisfaction were assessed from employees’ perceptions of customer-facing service outcomes rather than direct customer responses. Results indicate positive associations between AI-enabled HR practices and frontline employee engagement, and between engagement and employee-perceived customer service quality and satisfaction. Bootstrapped mediation analysis further indicates significant indirect pathways through frontline employee engagement. The findings extend AI-HRM research into the retail service context and highlight the importance of employee engagement in connecting AI-enabled HR practices with customer-facing service outcomes.

items.title: AI-Enabled Process Safety Digital Twin for Predictive Risk Management in Process Industries
items.abstract: Process safety management in process industries remains challenging due to complex operating conditions, equipment degradation, and limitations of conventional risk assessment methods. This study proposes a conceptual Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled process safety digital twin framework for predictive risk management. The architecture integrates real-time process monitoring, digital twin synchronization, machine learning-based anomaly detection, equipment reliability assessment, and dynamic risk prediction. An autoencoder is proposed for anomaly detection, while Long Short-Term Memory networks forecast process deviations and equipment degradation. A Dynamic Bayesian Network estimates evolving hazard probabilities using operational observations and predicted equipment conditions. The proposed evaluation protocol uses simulated industrial disturbances to assess detection accuracy, prediction lead time, false alarm rates, reliability estimation, and risk prediction performance. As the framework has not yet been implemented or experimentally validated, its potential benefits remain hypotheses requiring investigation. The study establishes a structured methodology for evaluating AI-assisted predictive safety decision support in industrial processing environments.

items.title: AI-Powered Entrepreneurship: A Critical Evidence Review and Unified Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Small Business Growth Prediction and Strategic Decision-Making
items.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics are increasingly transforming entrepreneurship by providing computational approaches to business-performance assessment, growth forecasting, and strategic decision-making. However, existing research remains fragmented across predictive modeling, explainability, uncertainty assessment, and practical decision-support applications, limiting the development of integrated and reliable analytical frameworks for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This study presents a structured critical evidence review and proposes a unified explainable machine-learning framework for small-business growth prediction and strategic decision-making. Methodology: The review draws on three Scopus literature searches covering publications from 2021 to 2026, yielding 917 unique bibliographic records after deduplication. Relevant studies were critically examined to identify methodological developments, research limitations, and requirements for theoretical integration. Findings: The synthesis highlights challenges involving inconsistent growth measures, temporal data limitations, model generalizability, explanation stability, predictive uncertainty, and the translation of forecasts into managerial decisions. In response, the study proposes a unified framework integrating enterprise-data preprocessing, machine-learning prediction, SHAP-based explainability, uncertainty assessment, and constraint-aware decision-support mechanisms. A complementary evaluation protocol specifies statistical benchmarks, temporal validation procedures, explanation-robustness measures, and decision-utility assessment. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The proposed framework contributes a structured methodological foundation for developing transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI-supported entrepreneurial analytics. Although its practical applications may support financial planning, resource allocation, and business-growth assessment, the framework remains conceptual and requires empirical implementation, independent validation, and real-world decision-impact evaluation.

items.title: AiWOM vs. influencer eWOM: an SOR perspective on source credibility and purchase intention
items.abstract: Introduction The growth of artificial intelligence in marketing has introduced AI-generated word of mouth (AiWOM) alongside influencer eWOM (IeWOM). Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework and Source Credibility Theory (SCT), this study compares the effects of AiWOM and IeWOM on purchase intention (PI) and examines the mediating role of source credibility. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with a verified sample of 562 active digital consumers aged 18 to 45 in Palestine, recruited through a combination of purposive and snowball sampling. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4, and the differences between the two sources were tested with bootstrapped paired-difference tests. Results Both human influencers and AI sources positively affected source credibility, but human influencers exerted a statistically significantly stronger effect on source credibility and purchase intention. Source credibility functioned as a complementary partial mediator for both IeWOM and AiWOM, with significant indirect effects coexisting with significant direct effects. Discussion Human influencers remain the more persuasive force in digital marketing, although AiWOM represents a viable emerging channel. By providing a formal, same-sample statistical comparison of human and AI eWOM within an integrated SOR-SCT model in an under-researched collectivist market, the study suggests that marketers should anchor credibility-building in human influencers while deploying AiWOM as a complementary, scalable channel.

items.abstract: ALAYA-999 is an independent research project investigating cross-model functional continuity, portable external memory, and verifiable cooperation between artificial intelligence systems. Experiment 003 presents an exploratory protocol involving six language models: Gemini, Claude, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, and Llama. The experiment recorded 16 substantive negotiation responses, 20 structured events, and 11 successful deterministic software tests. Four memory-card-assisted consultations successfully recovered both synthetic values and identified the blocked proposal. The proposed architecture incorporates versioned JSONL records, SHA-256 integrity verification, provenance tracking, conflict preservation, and human oversight. These preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of documentary information transfer across AI sessions and models. They do not establish artificial consciousness, persistent internal memory, or institutional partnerships. Independent researchers are invited to reproduce, criticize, and extend the experimental protocol. items.title: Algorithmic Fragility: How Organizations Stabilize Unstable Machines
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become embedded in organizational processes, they are widely celebrated for their precision and objectivity. Yet real-world deployments often reveal a different reality: algorithmic systems produce biased outputs, exhibit performance drift, and generate socially misaligned decisions, exposing their inherent instability. This paper extends the concept of algorithmic fragility to capture this persistent instability as a structural condition, not a temporary technical defect, arising from the interaction between machine learning properties and the socially complex environments in which these systems operate. To explain how organizations cope, we refine the concept of stabilization work: the distributed sociomaterial labor through which actors absorb, reinterpret, and manage algorithmic breakdowns to sustain the appearance of reliability. We identify three micro-level practices — buffering, reframing, and patching — and show how these become institutionalized into meso-level routines and macro-level legitimacy. The framework conceptualizes algorithmic fragility as constitutive rather than exceptional, advances stabilization work as a form of invisible organizational labor, and reframes AI governance as a continuous, practice-based accomplishment instead of ex ante technical control.

items.title: An Empirical Study of Stress Indicators among Students Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on students’ stress indicators, particularly perceived stress and its cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and physiological manifestations. The theoretical analysis re-vealed a lack of research addressing this issue, prompting an empirical study involving a sample of 102 stu-dents. The findings indicate that affective engagement with AI contributes to higher levels of perceived stress. At the same time, frequent use of AI reduces perceived stress levels while increasing its cognitive and emo-tional manifestations. Using the technology primarily for educational purposes increases the cognitive and be-havioral manifestations of stress. These results highlight the need to develop psychological programs to pre-vent stress resulting from the adverse effects of AI and to promote its psychologically safe use. They also un-derscore the need for further empirical research to identify other potential consequences of using this technol-ogy.

items.title: An examination of the impacts of ChatGPT-informed language instruction on EFL learners’ willingness to communicate, anxiety, autonomy, and self-regulated language learning
items.abstract: ChatGPT constitutes an Artificial Intelligence (AI) system that takes advantage of deep learning techniques to mimic human intelligence. This system has been used in language instruction due mainly to its favorable characteristics such as its availability and its personalized language teaching capability. Nonetheless, few studies have investigated its role in the amelioration of language learners’ psychological and self-regulatory factors. The present study aimed to examine the effects of ChatGPT-informed language instruction on Iranian EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate (WTC), Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety (FLCA), autonomy, and Self-Regulated Language Learning (SRLL). To this end, the researchers selected 50 intermediate-level female learners at a language institute as the participants and used a quasi-experimental design to conduct the study. Accordingly, they utilized pretests, ChatGPT-informed treatment sessions, and posttests to gather the data. In addition, they analyzed the obtained data using t-tests and the MANOVA test. The results of the study indicated that ChatGPT-informed language teaching significantly improved the participants’ WTC, autonomy, and SRLL. Additionally, it was effective in relieving the participants from their FLCA. The study discusses the implications of the results in foreign language contexts including the EFL context of Iran.

items.title: An integrative role-based multidimensional-motivational model of parent engagement and disaffection in child education
items.abstract: The importance of parent engagement for supporting children’s learning and academic success is well established and widely accepted. However, schools and teachers still often find it challenging to support and sustain such engagement. An updated understanding of how parents experience and enact their education-related roles may help to guide this work. To advance understanding and open up new directions for research this paper proposes an Integrative Role-Based Multidimensional-Motivational Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education. Taking a self-in-role perspective, the model proposes that parents invest and express themselves in the enactment of two distinct education-related roles: as co-educators supporting their child's educational experiences and needs, and as members of their child's school community. It specifies role-dependent multidimensional structures, with emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions in the co-educator role, and relational, psychological, and participatory dimensions in the school-community role. Within each role, engagement and disaffection are understood as related but distinct states. Disaffection includes withdrawal, but also reactive and resistant forms of role enactment, allowing some indicators of ‘over-involvement' to be distinguished from constructive engagement. The model further proposes that parent psychological need satisfaction supports engagement partly through autonomous motivation, whereas need frustration may contribute to disaffection; parents' beliefs about their educational roles are expected to shape these relationships. A central empirical test for future research is whether parent engagement and disaffection in the two roles explain children's own motivational experiences and subsequent educational and developmental outcomes beyond the frequency of parental involvement practices. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of the model's propositions for future research and educational practice.

items.title: Anxiety-calibrated generative-AI feedback for second language writing: the Cognition–Affect Dual-Adaptation model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can now deliver instant, detailed written corrective feedback on second language (L2) writing, but current systems deliver essentially the same message to every learner. We argue that this one-size-fits-all design neglects robust evidence that feedback effectiveness depends on learners’ emotional states—particularly writing anxiety. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes the Cognition–Affect Dual-Adaptation (CADA) model, which decomposes GAI feedback into a constant cognitive channel (error identification, explanation, and revision suggestions, identical for all learners) and an affective channel calibrated to the learner’s current anxiety tier (praise framing, mitigation intensity, and strength-first sequencing), with dynamic re-tiering as anxiety changes over time. Unlike existing adaptive-feedback frameworks, which adjust task difficulty or content selection, CADA leaves what is said untouched and adapts how it is said; and unlike ad hoc prompt-based personalization, it specifies the calibration rule, the psychological construct the rule responds to, and the conditions under which the rule itself should change. Integrating control–value theory, social cognitive theory, broaden-and-build theory, and feedback-literacy research, we advance six testable propositions: relative to uniform GAI feedback, CADA-calibrated feedback is predicted to (P1) reduce writing anxiety and (P2) increase writing self-efficacy; (P3) improve writing performance through a chained self-efficacy-to-anxiety mediation; (P4) yield compensatory benefits that are strongest for learners with high baseline anxiety; (P5) increase feedback uptake, which partially mediates performance gains; and (P6) produce self-correcting downward tier migration as within-person anxiety declines. We specify the model’s boundary conditions and a multi-phase research agenda spanning experimental, longitudinal, and process-tracing designs. The model proposes affect-responsive calibration as a candidate first-order design property of GAI writing tools and provides an integrative, falsifiable framework for research on emotion-adaptive feedback in L2 writing. If the propositions hold, emotional fit could become a specifiable, auditable property of every feedback message a learner receives—an outcome within reach of current GAI writing tools.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and enterprise value creation in human resources: A framework for strategic transformation
items.abstract: Organizations face mounting pressure to demonstrate measurable returns on artificial intelligence (AI) investments, yet evidence of sustained value creation remains uneven, particularly within human resources (HR), a function historically positioned as a cost center rather than a driver of enterprise performance. This article examines how AI can transform HR into a source of enterprise value, using IBM's AskHR platform as a primary case illustration. Building on documented outcomes that include a 40 percent reduction in HR operational costs, the automation of 94 percent of routine tasks, and 3.5 billion dollars in productivity improvements across 70 business units, the article demonstrates that strategically implemented AI in HR can simultaneously reduce costs, increase productivity, and enhance employee experience. To explain how these outcomes are achieved, the article develops a four lever value creation framework encompassing process redesign prior to automation, rapid iterative development, predefined performance measurement, and executive sponsorship. The analysis further shows that AI delivers the greatest organizational value when embedded within redesigned processes, integrated across enterprise systems, and deployed through hybrid human and AI operating models that augment rather than replace human judgment. The article contributes to scholarship on digital transformation and AI adoption by shifting focus from technology acquisition to value realization, and offers practical guidance for HR leaders and organizational managers seeking to align AI investments with long term enterprise performance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and HR Analytics in Strategic Human Resource Management: A Systematic Review of Workforce Agility
items.abstract: This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) that maps and synthesizes scholarly evidence on the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and human resource analytics (HR analytics) in strategic human resource management (SHRM) to strengthen workforce agility in a global context. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles through a structured search of the Scopus database covering publications from 2015 to 2025. The selection process included title and abstract screening, eligibility assessment, and study quality appraisal, resulting in 18 articles that met the inclusion criteria from 108 identified documents. Data were systematically extracted from abstracts and metadata and then analyzed using thematic synthesis to address RQ1–RQ4, including the mapping of technologies, SHRM practices, mechanisms, and agility-related outcomes. The findings indicate that AI and HR analytics tend to contribute to workforce agility through data-driven HR decision making, the strengthening of analytical capability, faster organizational responses, and competency development that supports adaptability. However, their effects depend on human readiness, data and AI governance, and human-centered work design. This review underscores that AI and HR analytics should be positioned as strategic capabilities within SHRM architecture and identifies directions for future research, particularly the need for more consistent workforce agility measurement, longitudinal and multi-level designs, and assessments of fairness and accountability in AI-enabled HR decision making.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotic Surgery: Understanding the Role of Trust and Attitude in Surgeons’ Behavioral Intention
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies play an important role in surgery. These technologies can support surgeons and help improve patient care. However, surgeons’ intention to use these technologies also depends on how they perceive them. This study aimed to identify the main factors associated with Romanian surgeons’ behavioral intention to use AI and robotic technologies in their professional practice. Methods: This quantitative study included 198 surgeons from Romania. Data were collected through an online questionnaire. A conceptual model was proposed, including six variables: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived compatibility, trust, attitude, and behavioral intention. The relationships between these variables were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with WarpPLS 8.0 software. Results: The hypotheses proposed in the conceptual model were supported, with statistically significant relationships. Trust showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.436), followed by attitude (β = 0.337). Perceived ease of use showed the strongest association with trust (β = 0.352). The proposed conceptual model explained 45.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of trust and attitude in Romanian surgeons’ behavioral intention to use AI and robotic technologies. They also suggest that professional training and improved access to these technologies may support their future adoption in surgical practice.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the changing work of healthcare professionals: a scoping review of work- and health-related outcomes
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly integrated into clinical practice and may reshape healthcare professionals' working conditions. Although research has primarily focused on clinical applications, diagnostic performance, and implementation, evidence on associations between AI use and healthcare professionals' work- and health-related outcomes remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map reported associations between AI use and six outcome domains among healthcare professionals in clinical settings: perceived stress, burnout, wellbeing, job satisfaction, social relationships, and interdisciplinary collaboration. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO were searched on August 12, 2025. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language empirical investigations of healthcare professionals who used or were directly affected by AI applications in real-world clinical settings and reported at least one outcome of interest. Study selection and data extraction were primarily conducted by one reviewer, with active machine learning supporting the screening. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively. Twenty-seven studies were included following database and backward citation searching. Job satisfaction, burnout, and perceived stress were examined most frequently, followed by wellbeing, social relationships, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Reported findings were mixed: some studies described favorable associations, including lower perceived stress and burnout, improved wellbeing, and higher job satisfaction, whereas others reported null, mixed, or unfavorable associations. Findings concerning social relationships and interdisciplinary collaboration were similarly heterogeneous. The evidence base was limited by variation in AI applications, populations, outcome measures, and study designs, reliance on observational evidence, short exposure periods in some studies, and the absence of a formal critical appraisal. The findings should therefore be interpreted as a map of reported associations rather than evidence that AI use improves healthcare professionals' work- or health-related outcomes. Longitudinal and qualitative research, including rigorous evaluation of implementation contexts and potential adverse effects, is needed to clarify how AI applications shape healthcare professionals' working conditions and wellbeing.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in forensic psychiatric risk assessment: opportunities, ethical challenges, and future directions
items.abstract: Risk assessment is a fundamental component of forensic psychiatric practice, informing decisions related to treatment planning, security measures, hospitalization, and legal proceedings. Traditional approaches rely on clinical interviews, historical information, and structured professional judgment instruments. However, their application may be affected by inter-rater variability, cognitive biases, and limitations in integrating complex information from multiple sources. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning have introduced new possibilities for forensic psychiatric risk assessment. These technologies can integrate multidimensional information, including electronic health records, sociodemographic characteristics, clinical variables, forensic histories, and behavioral indicators, potentially identifying patterns that may be difficult to recognize through conventional approaches. Nevertheless, their application raises substantial methodological, ethical, and legal concerns, particularly regarding algorithmic bias, explainability, data protection, accountability, and human oversight. This narrative review critically examines the potential applications of AI in forensic psychiatric risk assessment, with particular attention to the available evidence, methodological limitations, and ethical and legal implications. Although AI-based approaches show promise as decision-support tools, evidence supporting their clinical effectiveness, generalizability, and implementation in forensic psychiatric settings remains limited. Consequently, their use as autonomous decision-making systems cannot currently be justified. Future developments should prioritize transparent, explainable, auditable, and externally validated systems that support professional judgment while respecting fundamental rights and ethical principles.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become important for teachers’ professional development. This survey examined its relationships with lifelong learning tendency and teacher-perceived student development among 353 teachers engaged in mathematics gifted education in China. Four AI-literacy dimensions, two lifelong-learning dimensions, and a four-item teacher-perceived student-development score were analyzed. The outcome was adapted from an existing teacher-report framework. Analyses included reliability, separate and joint confirmatory factor models, discriminant-validity checks, correlations, hierarchical linear regression with HC3 robust inference, and repeated 10-fold cross-validation. Teacher-perceived student development showed internal consistency (alpha = .852; omega = .853) and a well-fitting one-factor model. Correlations with the six teacher characteristics were positive (r = .315−.359). The full regression explained 19.0% of the variance, with mean out-of-fold R 2 of .131. Lifelong learning added little beyond AI literacy (delta R 2 = .00075; robust block p = .845). AI perception had B = .180 (HC3 p = .0497; Holm-adjusted p = .298); none of the six focal coefficients was significant after Holm adjustment. This study documents positive associations of AI literacy and lifelong learning tendency with teacher-perceived student development, with overlapping explanatory contributions in the combined model. These findings identify AI literacy and lifelong learning as interrelated professional attributes relevant to teacher-perceived student development in mathematics gifted education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Utilization: Exploring Competence, Access, and Attitudes of Public School Teachers
items.abstract: This study examined public school teachers’ artificial intelligence (AI) utilization competence, access to AI resources, and attitudes toward AI use in instructional planning in the Baliwasan District, Zamboanga City, during School Year 2026–2027. Using a quantitative descriptive-comparative and correlational design, the study surveyed 83 teachers from selected elementary, junior high, and senior high schools, identified through purposive sampling, who participated voluntarily. Data were collected through Google Forms using a researcher-developed questionnaire subjected to expert validation and pilot testing among 30 teachers excluded from the main sample. Analyses included the arithmetic mean, one-way analysis of variance, and the r-value. Teachers reported high AI utilization competence and access, alongside positive to very positive attitudes, although connectivity during working hours and institution-supported resources emerged as relative constraints. No statistically significant differences were detected by teaching level. Conventional ANOVA identified differences across years-in-service groups for all three outcomes and across educational-attainment groups for competence and attitudes, but not access; these remained provisional because of small, unequal subgroups and variance violations. AI utilization competence and AI access were strongly and positively associated with attitudes, although these associations do not establish causation. The study concludes that teachers’ attitudes toward AI in instructional planning are closely linked to their competence and access. It recommends needs-based professional learning, dependable technological resources, and practical guidance on responsible AI use. As evidence from a nonprobability sample, the results inform context-specific planning rather than population-wide conclusions.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED PERSONALIZED LEARNING AND INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS FOR PROGRAMMING EDUCATION: A REVIEW
items.abstract: Writing programs calls for logical thinking, regular practice and useful feedback, since together they develop computational thinking and problem-solving skill. Yet many novices find concepts hard to absorb, cannot easily trace their own mistakes and falter as exercises grow more demanding, while standard classroom teaching rarely adjusts support to what each student already knows or how fast they progress. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being adopted to narrow this gap through personalised learning environments and intelligent tutoring systems. The present review examines AI-supported personalised programming education, covering intelligent tutors, AI coding assistants, automated code assessment, adaptive learning and individualised feedback. It describes how machine learning, natural language processing and large language models assist students by spotting mistakes, clarifying concepts, generating contextaware hints and suggesting fitting tasks. The influence of gamification, interactive coding environments and gradually rising difficulty on motivation and steady practice is also discussed. These advantages are balanced against drawbacks: the dependability of generated feedback, excessive reliance on AI support, data privacy and academic integrity. By comparing existing approaches and the gaps between them, the review presents a consolidated view of how personalised and tutoring systems can aid programming education and indicates future work on trustworthy, learner-centred systems that pair automated support with independent problem solving.

items.title: Association of AI Academic Dependency and AI Self-Efficacy with Clinical Reasoning Among Clinical Practicum Students with Experience Using Generative AI: The Role of AI Ethical Awareness
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the mediating and moderating roles of AI ethical awareness in the relationships of AI academic dependency and AI self-efficacy with clinical reasoning among clinical practicum students with experience using generative AI. Methods: This cross-sectional survey study included 135 students from a university in Daejeon, South Korea. Participants were university students who had used generative AI for academic purposes and had completed a clinical practicum within the previous six months. Data were collected using an online questionnaire on Google Forms between 17 June and 6 July 2026. Results: AI ethical awareness showed evidence consistent with significant mediating (indirect effect = −0.047, 95% CI: −0.089 to −0.010) and moderating (B = −0.012, p = 0.015, ΔR2 = 0.039) roles in the association between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning. However, in the association between AI self-efficacy and clinical reasoning, neither the mediating (indirect effect = −0.018, 95% CI: −0.054 to 0.008) nor the moderating (interaction B = 0.004, p = 0.339) roles of AI ethical awareness were significant. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that AI ethical awareness is associated with the relationship between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning, potentially serving as both a mediator and a moderator. The negative association between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning varies according to the level of AI ethical awareness. Future studies are needed to explore the complex role of AI ethical awareness and to determine how educational interventions related to AI ethics may influence students’ learning and clinical reasoning processes.

items.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
items.abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

items.title: Beyond Digital Representation: LLM-Assisted Human–AI Collaborative Design for Emotional Experience in Architectural Heritage
items.abstract: The digitization of architectural heritage should go beyond spatial reconstruction and information presentation. It should also help users develop emotional connections with cultural content. This study explores an LLM-assisted human–AI collaborative design approach to emotional experience in digital architectural heritage. The study uses Liu Bei Hall and its surrounding spaces at Chengdu Wuhou Shrine as a case study. Based on architectural and cultural materials and user needs, the study identifies four design dimensions: spatial exploration, contextual narrative, interactive feedback, and experience pacing. The researchers developed three desktop-based prototypes and evaluated them with 164 participants. The unadjusted analysis showed significantly higher emotional engagement in the LLM-assisted condition than in the information-presentation condition. However, this difference became smaller and was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for covariates. All four design dimensions were significantly positively correlated with emotional engagement, and the four-factor regression model explained 53.7% of its variance. Interactive feedback showed the strongest independent association with emotional engagement, while contextual narrative also retained a significant positive association. Follow-up interviews further highlighted the importance of coordinating spatial exploration, cultural narrative, interactive feedback, and experience pacing to create coherent digital heritage experiences. These findings suggest that LLMs can support design thinking, content organization, and iterative development. Their main value lies in assisting human designers rather than replacing them.

items.title: Beyond Licensure: The Bonaparte Nursing Practice Readiness–Quality Outcomes Theory—An Integrated Middle‐Range Framework for Measurement, Implementation, and Workforce Impact
items.abstract: AIM: To introduce the proposed Bonaparte Nursing Practice Readiness-Quality Outcomes Theory, distinguish practice readiness from related constructs, and describe its implications for assessment and patient safety. DESIGN: Conceptual nursing theory development through a critical synthesis of seven bodies of scholarship. METHODS: Seven scholarly foundations-Tanner's Clinical Judgement Model, Benner's Novice-to-Expert Framework, the NCSBN Clinical Judgement Measurement Model, QSEN competencies, Donabedian's Quality Framework, human factors theory, and implementation science-were compared within four thematic clusters. Nine proposed readiness domains and a four-phase research program for developing and evaluating the Practice Readiness Assessment Tool (PRAT) are described. RESULTS: The proposed middle-range theory defines practice readiness as an integrated, context-dependent nursing capacity expressed through clinical decision-making, with contextual conditions moderating its hypothesized relationships with patient and system outcomes. The nine-domain structure, theoretical relationships, and PRAT measurement properties remain unvalidated and require empirical testing. NO PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No patients or members of the public participated in this conceptual theory-development article. Future empirical studies will require appropriate research oversight and consideration of patient and public involvement.

items.title: Beyond Technology: Cybersecurity Governance And Human Capacity In AI-Enabled Education — Evidence From A Burundian Secondary School
items.abstract: As schools in low-resource settings adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) for personalized learning, they simultaneously take on cybersecurity risks that are rarely examined in the AI-in-education literature. This study investigated the cybersecurity challenges associated with AI adoption at Discovery School, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi. A convergent mixed-methods design combined a structured survey (n = 110: administrators, teachers, students, parents) with semi-structured interviews (n = 35), analyzed in SPSS 27 (descriptive statistics, chi-square test) and NVivo 14 (six-phase thematic analysis, Cohen's κ = 0.83), triangulated through a joint-display approach and interpreted through the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Cybersecurity readiness was rated only moderately overall (M = 3.19, SD = 0.84) against a backdrop of high perceived AI effectiveness for learning (M = 3.98). Counter-intuitively, administrators (the group with the fullest institutional view) reported the lowest confidence of any stakeholder group (M = 2.80), which is interpreted as informed awareness of governance gaps rather than technical incompetence. A chi-square test confirmed a statistically significant association between having received cybersecurity training and confidence in managing AI-related security risks, χ²(1) = 8.09, p = .004. Qualitative analysis identified Cybersecurity Awareness and Practices as a major theme (16.3% of coded references, 27 interviewees), revealing unclear data-ownership provisions in third-party vendor contracts, the absence of a formal incident-reporting procedure, and a near-total absence of student voice in cybersecurity discussions. Triangulation indicated that the school's central cybersecurity vulnerability is institutional and human rather than purely technological: awareness exists, but detection, response, and recovery capacity does not. items.title: Beyond the Weakest Link: A Critical Integrative Review of Human Factors in Cybersecurity, 2000-2025
items.abstract: Background: The weakest-link metaphor treats security failure as an individual deficit and underweights the work systems that shape performance. Purpose: This review examined how human factors scholarship in cybersecurity developed from 2000 through July 2025, which mechanisms recur across evidence traditions, and which operational practices remain robust under evidence-role sensitivity testing. Method: The study conducted a bounded retrospective integrative review of 69 preserved evidence sources. The author reconciled every included source against the reference list, separated 40 primary empirical studies from 29 secondary, conceptual, methodological, and contextual sources, applied a design-sensitive appraisal, and used chronological, domain, tension, and practice coding. Four sensitivity analyses tested the findings using only primary empirical sources, only peer-reviewed sources, substantial primary evidence, and a corpus that excluded author-involved sources. The study treats retained search strings as provenance rather than as proof of an exhaustive historical search. Results: The corpus widened its unit of analysis from the individual at an interface to the employee within policy, the workforce within a sociotechnical system, and the analyst within a human-AI team. Five interacting domains and four recurring tensions organized the evidence. Control-work fit, behaviorally grounded role-specific learning, and layered social-engineering resilience retained strong convergence. Work-system risk and adaptive resilience retained moderate convergence. Cumulative demand and reporting systems remained moderate-emerging, and AI reliance calibration remained emerging. Excluding non-peer-reviewed and author-involved sources did not change the practice ratings. Conclusion: The Human Factors Cybersecurity Systems Framework links system levels, human performance mechanisms, practices, moderators, outcomes, and feedback. The framework offers an auditable explanatory structure and an evaluation agenda, but it does not constitute a validated predictive model or universal maturity scale. Keywords: Human Factors, Cybersecurity, Human-Centered Cybersecurity, Usable Security, Security Fatigue, Sociotechnical Resilience, Human-AI Teaming, Integrative Review, Sensitivity Analysis

items.title: Building Intelligent Ethical Governance in the AI Era through AI-Based Prophetic Leadership for Institutional Transformation
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has accelerated institutional transformation through data analysis capabilities, process automation, and technology-based decision-making support. However, the increasing use of AI also presents ethical challenges related to transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, and human responsibility in controlling technology. This study aims to explore how AI-Enabled Prophetic Leadership contributes to building Smart Ethical Governance to support sustainable institutional transformation. This study uses an exploratory qualitative approach involving 24 participants from three institutions that have implemented AI-based digital transformation. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results of the study show three main findings, namely: (1) the reconstruction of prophetic leadership values (shiddiq, amanah, tabligh, and fathanah) into dimensions of digital integrity, moral accountability, communicative transparency, and ethical intelligence; (2) the integration of prophetic leadership and AI through human-centered decision-making, algorithmic oversight, system transparency, and strengthening organizational competencies; and (3) institutional transformation through structural, cultural, and operational changes. This research produces a conceptual model of the AI-Based Prophetic Ethical Governance Model (APEGM) that positions prophetic leadership as the foundation of values, AI as a decision-support instrument, and human oversight as a technology control mechanism. This research provides theoretical contributions to the development of ethical leadership and AI governance studies and provides practical implications for institutions in building innovative, responsible, and human-value-oriented digital transformations.
